question.text: Which candidate will lead Alaska's U.S. Senate race in first-choice votes as of November 13, 2026?
question.resolution_criteria: This question resolves based on the Alaska Division of Elections' cumulative unofficial first-choice vote totals for U.S. Senator in the 2026 General Election, as displayed on its Election Night Reporting page (https://www.elections.alaska.gov/results/26GENR/) in the most recent update posted at or before 11:59 p.m. AKST on November 13, 2026 (08:59 UTC on November 14). The option naming the candidate whose displayed total is highest resolves YES, and all other options resolve NO; if two or more candidates are tied for the highest total, "Any other candidate" resolves YES. Candidates are identified by the Division's own labels on that page ("Heikes, Gerald L.", "Peltola, Mary", "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.", "Sullivan, Dan S."), and any candidate or write-in total not matching one of the named options falls under "Any other candidate". Because the page is overwritten cumulatively, an archived capture of the page (for example a Wayback Machine snapshot) showing the totals in effect at that cutoff may be used to establish them. If the totals cannot be recovered from that page or its archived captures, [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) will be used.
question.fine_print: "First-choice votes" means the round-one totals reported for each candidate before any ranked-choice tabulation; ranked-choice transfer rounds (scheduled for November 18, 2026) and the eventual winner of the seat are not used. Litigation or court orders concerning certification of the election, including United States of America v. State of Alaska, No. 3:26-cv-00376-SLG (D. Alaska), do not affect this question.

## Alaska U.S. Senate race: who leads first-choice votes as of Nov. 13, 2026 (research only, no forecast)

### 1. Resolution source
- 2026-11-02: I couldn't fetch the Division of Elections results page (https://www.elections.alaska.gov/results/26GENR/) because of a certificate error ("unable to verify the first certificate"). The question background says the page lists all four Senate candidates at zero votes until the election. That is expected, since voting ends November 3. I could not check it directly.
- Ballots by mail within the U.S. must arrive by November 13. Counting and first-choice reporting continue November 4 to 17, and the ranked-choice tabulation runs November 18 (from the Division's media packet, as summarized in the question). Some ballots will still be uncounted at the November 13 cutoff.

### 2. Current status
- 2026-11-02: No votes have been reported. Nothing settles the question yet.
- 2026-11-01: Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit. She ruled the government lacked standing because a court order could not fix its claimed injury, and she called the requested relief "infeasible" because many people had already voted. The DOJ says it will appeal. Separate federal criminal and state investigations into how the second Sullivan was recruited are still open. Under the question's terms, none of this affects how it resolves. [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/01/alaska-senate-doj-lawsuit-dismissed-sullivan-peltola.html); [Alaska Public Media](https://alaskapublic.org/news/politics/elections/2026-11-01/judge-tosses-doj-lawsuit-that-sought-to-block-election-results-if-republican-sen-dan-sullivan-loses); [Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/judge-trump-alaska-senate-election-dan-sullivan-12647199)

### 3. Recent news (newest first)
- 2026-11-02: Reason reports that the New York Times said Peltola's campaign was involved in encouraging Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.'s candidacy. Peltola's campaign and the DSCC (the Senate Democrats' campaign committee) deny recruiting him. [Reason](https://reason.com/2026/11/02/ranked-choice-voting-will-untangle-alaskas-dan-sullivan-controversy-its-also-on-the-ballot-itself/); [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/01/alaska-senate-doj-lawsuit-dismissed-sullivan-peltola.html)
- 2026-11-02: CBS reports that four candidates are on the ballot: Dan S. Sullivan, Peltola, Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan. [CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ranked-choice-ballot-alaska-senate-dan-sullivan/)
- 2026-10-30 (approx.): The latest Alaska Survey Research poll has Peltola ahead 48% to 46% on first choices. [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/01/alaska-senate-doj-lawsuit-dismissed-sullivan-peltola.html)
- 2026-10-27: The state of Alaska and Peltola's campaign moved to dismiss the DOJ suit. [Alaska Beacon](https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/10/27/alaska-fights-back-against-trump-ordered-elections-lawsuit-seeks-its-dismissal/)
- 2026-10-23: The DOJ sued to block certification if Peltola wins. [Alaska Beacon](https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/10/23/trump-administration-sues-to-block-alaskas-us-senate-election-result-if-peltola-wins/)

### 4. Base rates: how leads moved after election night
- 2022 Senate race: Tshibaka led on election night by about 7 points. The gap closed as rural ballots and later absentee ballots came in. Around November 14 it stood at 43.3% Tshibaka to 43.1% Murkowski, out of roughly 240,000 counted. Alaska Public Media dated Murkowski's first-choice lead to Friday, November 18 (112,519 to 110,861). That means the election-night leader was still narrowly ahead around the equivalent of the November 13 cutoff, and the lead flipped later. [Peninsula Clarion](https://peninsulaclarion.com/news/murkowski-tshibaka-in-dead-heat-peltola-inches-toward-50-in-latest-election-results); [Alaska Public Media](https://alaskapublic.org/news/2022-11-18/murkowski-takes-lead-in-alaskas-u-s-senate-race); [Juneau Empire](https://www.juneauempire.com/?p=93002)
- 2024 House race: Begich led Peltola about 49% to 45% on election night. On November 16 it was 48.7% to 46.1%, a lead of more than 8,300 votes. Later ballots moved slightly toward Peltola, but the leader never changed. [Alaska's News Source](https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2024/11/21/alaska-chooses-keep-ranked-choice-voting-begich-defeats-peltola-unofficial-results-show/?outputType=amp); [ADN](https://adn.com/politics/2024/11/15/key-alaska-election-results-largely-unchanged-as-thousands-of-additional-ballots-are-counted)
- 2022 House race: Peltola led first-choice votes from election night onward. [ADN](https://adn.com/politics/2022/11/08/peltola-leads-alaskas-us-house-race-in-early-results)
- The pattern: ballots counted after election night (mail, absentee and remote rural) have tended to shift results a few points toward Democrats or Murkowski-style candidates. Alaska Beacon's James Brooks has described the same tendency. In those years, the shift by mid-November was about 1 to 3 points.
- 2026 primary (August 18): Peltola led first-choice votes 49.5% to 41.4%, with Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 2.5% (from the question background). Neither Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. nor Heikes has polled anywhere near the lead.
- Turnout: as of October 30, 78,090 ballots had been received. The 2022 general election had about 260,000 first-choice Senate votes.

### 5. Other forecasts
- Kalshi, Peltola's first-round vote share: "at least 46%" 0.85, "at least 47%" 0.69, "at least 48%" 0.51, "at least 50%" 0.17. These markets settle on final results, not the November 13 count, so they are a close but not exact match.
- Kalshi: turnout above 290,000 at 0.58. Polymarket: Alaska race within 5% at 0.665.
- Manifold: "Sullivan wins re-election" at 30% and 29%. This is about the final ranked-choice winner, not first-choice votes on November 13.
- Kalshi, "reddest state to elect a Democrat": Alaska at 0.06. This is not directly comparable, because the market pays on the reddest state, so Kansas and others absorb the probability.
- Cook Political Report rates the race a Toss Up (October 30).
- Senate control: Democrats about 0.73 on both Kalshi and Polymarket.
- I found no market on first-choice votes as of November 13 specifically.

### 6. Upcoming events before resolution
- 2026-11-03: Election Day. First results that night will cover polling-place ballots plus early votes cast October 19 to 29.
- 2026-11-04 to 11-13: Ongoing count updates. The November 13 mail-receipt deadline means some late absentee ballots, which have historically leaned left, may not be counted until after the cutoff.
- Possible DOJ appeal of the dismissal. It doesn't affect the count.
- A near-tie on election night would make the November 13 snapshot sensitive to the order in which batches are counted (rural, absentee, questioned ballots).
- Votes for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. could take a few points from the incumbent's first-choice total. The primary benchmark was 2.5%.

forecasts.reasoning:
**(a) Time left:** Voting ends November 3. The resolving snapshot is the last update at or before 11:59 p.m. AKST on November 13, so about 11 to 12 days remain. Most ballots will be counted by then. Some late absentee and questioned ballots, which have historically leaned left, may not be.

**(b) Status quo:** No votes have been reported yet. The best guide to where things stand is the polling and the primary: Peltola led the August primary 49.5% to 41.4%, and the latest Alaska Survey Research poll (October 26 to 29) has her ahead 48% to 46% on first choices. The status quo leans Peltola, but only narrowly.

**(c) Base rates:** In recent Alaska federal races, the election-night leader usually still led at the mid-November mark.
- 2022 Senate: Tshibaka was still barely ahead of Murkowski around November 14 and lost the lead on November 18.
- 2024 House: Begich led throughout.
- 2022 House: Peltola led throughout.

Ballots counted after election night shift results about 1 to 3 points toward Democrats or moderate candidates. Minor candidates never lead. A first-choice leader in a top-four race is essentially always one of the two major candidates.

**(d) Strongest evidence:**
- ASR poll, October 26 to 29: Peltola 48%, Sullivan 46% on first choices.
- Kalshi prices Peltola's first-round share at "at least 48%" 0.51 and "at least 47%" 0.69. That implies a median near 48%, with roughly 4 to 6% going to Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and Heikes combined.
- Manifold gives Sullivan about 30% to win the final ranked-choice count.
- Ranked-choice transfers from Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. likely favor the incumbent. So Peltola's first-choice lead should be somewhat more likely than her winning the final count.
- Cook Political Report rated the race a Toss Up on October 30.
- The DOJ lawsuit was dismissed on November 1 and is irrelevant to this question anyway.

**(e) Unexpected scenario:**
- Polls in Alaska have sometimes underestimated Republicans, as in 2024. Sullivan could lead on election night by 4 or more points, and late ballots might not close the gap by November 13.
- Alternatively, the race could be a near-tie where batch timing decides who leads at the cutoff.
- Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. leading is essentially impossible. An exact tie for "Any other candidate" is negligibly likely.

**Adjustment:** I start from roughly 70% Peltola to win the final count, based on the market and Manifold. I move up slightly because ranked-choice transfers hurt her, so her first-choice lead is likelier than her win. I then move back down because some Democratic-leaning late ballots may not be counted by November 13, and because Alaska polls have historically missed Republican strength. The net is about 69% Peltola.

Option_A: 0.29
Option_B: 0.69
Option_C: 0.01

(b) **Status quo:** No votes have been counted. The best available "current state" is the polling and the primary:
- Alaska Survey Research (October 26-29) has Peltola ahead 48% to 46% on first choices.
- In the August primary, Peltola led 49.5% to 41.4%.

If nothing changes, Peltola leads first-choice votes.

(c) **Base rates:** In recent Alaska federal races, the first-choice leader around mid-November has usually been whoever led overall:
- 2022 Senate: the election-night leader (Tshibaka) was still narrowly ahead around the November 13-14 equivalent, and the lead flipped to Murkowski later.
- 2024 House and 2022 House: the leader never changed.

Late-counted ballots tend to move results 1 to 3 points toward the less conservative candidate. That favors Peltola if the race is close on election night. Fringe candidates such as Heikes or Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. have essentially no record of leading statewide first-choice counts. Sullivan Jr. got 2.5% in the primary.

(d) **Strongest evidence:**
- Kalshi's market on Peltola's first-round share (November 2) prices her at about 51% to reach at least 48%, 69% for at least 47%, and 85% for at least 46%. That is a median near 48%. With Sullivan Jr. and Heikes likely taking roughly 3 to 5% combined, Dan S. Sullivan's first-choice share would sit around 45 to 47%.
- The ASR poll (October 26-29) shows Peltola up 2 on first choices.
- Manifold puts Sullivan's chance of winning the final ranked-choice count at about 30%. Peltola's first-choice lead should be at least as likely as her final win, because Sullivan Jr.'s transfers mostly help the incumbent.
- Cook rates the race a Toss Up (October 30).
- The DOJ suit was dismissed on November 1. It is irrelevant to resolution anyway.

I start from roughly 70% Peltola, which is the market-implied final win probability. I move only slightly up for the vote-splitting effect of the duplicate surname, and slightly down for Alaska's history of Republicans outperforming polls. These roughly offset.

(e) **Unexpected scenario:** Polls underestimate Republican turnout, as has often happened in Alaska. Dan S. Sullivan then leads by 3 or more points on election night, and the late ballots counted by November 13 are not enough to close the gap. Less plausibly, a data-entry or reporting glitch on the Division's page, or a dead-tie display, could produce an odd result. That is why I keep small residual probabilities on the other two options.
